lawyer:
Morshed Ahmed Khan, Advocate—For the Petitioners. 
Sayeda Afsar Jahan, Deputy Attorney-General—For the Respondents.
parties:
Mahbubul Haque Sikder ------ Petitioners 
vs 
Commissioner of Customs & others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
AFM Abdur Rahman J: The petitioner obtained the instant Rule calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned orders dated 14-6-1998, 25-6-1998 and 28-6-1998 issued by the respondent No. 1 imposing 150% supplementary duty as per Finance Act, 1998 (Annexure A) on the importation of Volvo Cars by the petitioners should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the respondents should not be directed to calculate the duties and taxes in respect of the said imported vehicles of the petitioners as per Finance Act, 1997 imposing such tax @ 60%.

2. It has been asserted in the writ petition that the petitioner, being the partner of Messrs Al Traders, is the sole agent in Bangladesh for the world famous 'Volvo Cars' made in Sweden. The petitioner's firm has been duly registered with the office of the Chief Controller of Imports and Exports as importer and obtained Import Registration No. Ba. 51472 on 13-10-1997. The petitioner in course of their business established a letter of credit No. 01-261-97 on 15-10-1997 through Prime Bank Limited, Motijheel Branch, Dhaka in favour of Messrs Volvo Car International for importation of 15 Units Volvo Cars from Sweden for an amount of US$ 3,94,500. The supplier Messrs Volvo Car International pursuant to the said letter of credit supplied 12 units Volvo Cars by three consignments. The first consignment of 6 units Volvo Cars were shipped on board of the vessel MV Sovereign Maersk on 21-11-1997 and six bills of lading Nos. GOT035615, GOT035617, GOT035619, GOT035734, GOT035737, and GOT035739 all dated 21-11-1997 were issued. The second consignment of 2 units Volvo Cars were shipped on board of the Vessel MV Knud Maersk on 28-11-1997 and two bills of lading Nos. GOT035374 and GOT035805 all dated 28-11-1997 were issued. The third consignment of 4 units Volvo Cars were shipped on board of the Vessel MV Kristen Mearsk on 5-12-1997 and four bills of lading Nos. GOT035727, GOT036043, GOT036044 and GOT036050 all dated 5-12-1997 were issued. All those consignments were loaded from the port of Gothenburg, Sweden with destination to Chittagong and the place of delivery was ICD, Kamlapur, Dhaka. These three consignments reached ICD, Kamlapur, Dhaka within the month of December, 1997 and January, 1998. The petitioners through their clearing agent Messrs Azad Traders submitted bills of entries along with relevant documents in order to release six units Volvo cars out of 12 units Volvo Cars. The petitioners paid 42.5% customs duty, 60% supplementary duty, 15% VAT, AIT 2.5% L Fees and 2.5% IDSC and released those six units of Volvo Cars on 19-1-1998, 26-10-1998, 1-6-1998, 25-6-1998 covered by bills of lading Nos. GOT035615, GOT035619, GOT035734, GOT035739, GOT035727 and GOT036044 respectively.

3. The further case of the petitioners is that they could not obtain release of the remaining cars expeditiously as the Customs Authority had asked for manufacturer's price and other information and the petitioner has to spend time for collection of those documents and information to satisfy the queries of the Customs Authority. Subsequently, the petitioners on 16-6-1998 through their clearing agent Messrs Azad Traders submitted further six bills of entry Nos. 06891, 06892, 06893, 06895 and 06896 along with relevant documents to release the remaining six units of Volvo Cars covered under the bills of lading Nos. GOT035637, GOT035617, GOT036043, GOT036050, GOT035374 and GOT035805. But the respondents, Customs Authority, calculated the duties and taxes along with 150% supplementary duty as per Finance Act, 1998 instead of 60% of such as per the Finance Act, 1997 although the bills of entry were submitted long before the Finance Act, 1998 came into effect. The petitioner challenging such imposition of enhanced supplementary duty as per the Finance Act, 1998 preferred this writ petition and obtained the Rule Nisi.

4. The Rule is duly served upon the respondents and the learned Deputy Attorney-General, Ms Sayeda Afsar Jahan appeared on behalf of the respondents but did not prefer any affidavit-in-opposition.

5. The learned Advocate Mr Morshed Ahmed Khan, appearing for the petitioner, after taking us through the various Annexures appended to the writ petition, submits that the petitioner imported altogether 12 units Volvo Cars under the same letter of credit through three consignments which reached ICD, Kamalapur in the month of December, 1997 and January, 1998 out of which the petitioner released six units of Volvo Cars by submitting different bills of entry. But subsequently, when the petitioner attempted to release the remaining six units Volvo Cars and filed the bills of entry in time, the respondent, with an ulterior motive, did not receive the bills of entry for the remaining cars till budget for 1998 was tabled in the parliament and till the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act was amended to include the enhanced rate of supplementary duty upon the importation of those cars by the petitioner. Mr Ahmed categorically submits that although the petitioner through his C&F agent attempted to submit the bills of entry as soon as the consignment reached the ICD, Kamlapur, Dhaka, the respondents did not register the same till 16-6-1998. The learned Advocate in support of his contention has taken us to the dates of shipment of the consignments and its arrival at ICD, Kamlapur and concluded that if the respondents were not driven by an ulterior motive, the petitioner could effect release of the entire goods much earlier than, the imposition of enhanced rate of supplementary duty on the importation of the cars by the petitioner Mr Ahmed, finally, submits that the petitioner had been forced to undergo financial prejudice by the respondents for which his right to be treated in accordance with law has been violated for which the petitioner is entitled to the relief as prayed for.

6. On the other hand, the learned Deputy Attorney-General Mrs Sayeda Afsar Jahan, advanced argument against the contentions of the petitioner regarding an ulterior motive and submits that the petitioner failed to substantiate his grounds of objection by any cogent and material documents for which the petitioner is not entitled to any relief as prayed for.

7. We have heard the learned Advocate, perused the writ petition and the Annexures appended thereto. We have also examined the relevant law and the SRO, the bills of entry submitted by the petitioner and also perused the Customs file which was called for by this Court to ascertain the actual date of submission of the bills of entry to the Customs Authority. We have considered the arguments advanced at the Bar.

8. The petitioner mainly contends, that although the three consignments containing 12 units Volvo Cars had been reached much earlier than the enhancement of the supplementary duty by the Finance Act, 1998 and the collection of it by the effect of Provisional Collection of Taxes Act from 1st June, 1998, yet the respondents with an ulterior motive to collect more duties from the petitioner has dragged the receiving of bills of entry from the petitioner to a date when the budget for 1998 was tabled in the Parliament proposing enhanced rate of supplementary duty. To appreciate this contention, it is required to examine the exact date of filing of bills of entry for which this Court called for the relevant Customs Nothi and accordingly, the same has been perused by this Court.

9. Admittedly, in the month of January, 1998 there was no system for electronic filing of bill of entry for which the filing date of bill of entry has to be ascertained from the receiving seal affixed at the bill of entry. It appears that affixing of this receiving seal in the body of the bill of entry is the exercise of the respondents Customs Authority and the person who is submitting the bill of entry had no weapon to compel the Customs Authority to affix the receiving seal immediately at its submission and there appears to exist a scope to delay in affixing this receiving seal on the body of the document in accordance with the sweet will of the receiving authority. Mr Ahmed, vigorously argued that the C&F agent of the petitioner attempted to submit the bill of entry for the remaining six units of Volvo Cars in the month of January, 1998 as soon as the consignments reached ICD, Kamalapur but the respondents primarily, on the ground of insufficient documents and thereafter, on an ulterior motive, did not receive the same till 16-6-1998.

10. It appears from the Annexure C, which is the letter of credit No. 01-261-97 opened through Prime Bank Limited, Moulvibazar Branch, Dhaka, that the petitioner under the said letter of credit proposed to import altogether 15 units of Volvo $ 90 Sweden Car of different colours and the same were shipped from Gothenburg, Sweden through the shipping company Maersk Line. The supplier Messrs Volvo Car International Limited supplied 12 units Volvo cars through three consignments. From Annexure D, it appears that the first consignment containing six units of Volvo Cars was shipment on board the vessel MV Sovereign Maersk on 21-11-1997 and six bills of lading being Nos. GOT035615, GOT035617, GOT035619, GOT035734, GOT035737, and GOT035739 all dated 21-11-1997 were issued. This first consignment reached ICD Kamlapur, Dhaka on 31-12-1997 and the petitioner effected release of four units of Volvo Cars of the first consignment covered by bills of lading Nos. GOT035615, GOT035619, GOT035734 and GOT035739 dated 19-1-1998 out of total six unit cars. The second consignment containing two units Volvo Cars, was shipped on board the vessel MV Knud Maersk on 28-11-1997 and two bills of lading being No. GOT035374 and GOT035805 both dated 28-11-1997 were issued which reached ICD, Kamlapur, Dhaka, in the month of January, 1998 but the petitioner did not take release of the cars of this 2nd consignment. The third consignment containing four units Volvo Cars was shipped on board the vessel MV Kristen Maersk on 5-12-1997 and four bills of entry Nos. GOT035727, GOT036043, GOT036044 and GOT036050 all dated 5-12-1997 were issued which reached ICD, Kamlapur, Dhaka, on 18-1-1998. The petitioner effected release of two cars out of 3rd consignment covered under the bills of lading No. GOT035727 and GOT036044 but did not effect release of remaining six units Volvo Cars two from 1st consignment, total two of the 2nd consignment and two from 3rd consignment. The contention of the petitioner is that he could not effect the release of the remaining six units Volvo Cars due to the non-receipt of bills of entry by the Customs Authority till 16-6-1998, and such, non-receipt of bills of entry is evident from the fact that the respondents did not take step under section 82 of the Customs Act, 1969 in respect of putting the cars on sale through auction after the laps of statutory period to effect release of consignment.

11. We do not find any substance in the contention of the petitioner mainly for two reasons.

12. Firstly, the petitioner contends that he could not effect release of six units Volvo Cars due to non-receipt of bills of entry by the respondents till 16-6-1998 though the same was submitted much earlier and the respondents with an ulterior motive wanted some superfluous documents which compelled the petitioner to collect the same at the cost of time. This contention appears to be devoid of any basis, since the petitioner effected release of four units Volvo Cars from the 1st and two units of Volvo Cars from the 3rd consignment of the same make, same engine and some model. If the petitioner could effect release of six units of Volvo Cars out of ten units Volvo Cars of two consignments of the same particulars then, the story of asking for some superfluous documents of the same class cars does not hold any water.

13. The learned Deputy Attorney-General strenuously argued that the petitioner did not voluntarily take release of the six units Volvo Cars due to his miscalculated aspiration that ensuing budget will reduce the duty on import of cars but when to his prejudice the rate of supplementary duty has been enhanced, the petitioner invented the story of non-receipt of bills of entry in time and now comes up with a fictitious story of malafide through the supplementary affidavit about which not an iota of fact is mentioned in the original writ petition.

14. We find substance in the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General as it appears from the relevant Customs Nothi, which this Court called for, that the petitioner submitted the bills of entry for releasing the four units Volvo Cars from the 1st consignment on 18-1-1998 covered by bills of lading Nos. GOT035615, GOT035619, GOT035734 and GOT035739 and the same was released on 19-1-1998, 19-1-1998, 19-1-1998 and 26-1-1998 respectively after observing all the legal formalities. Thereafter, the petitioner submitted bills of entry for releasing two units Volvo Cars from the 3rd consignment on 29-4-1998 covered by bills of lading No. GOT035727 and GOT036044 and the same was released on 1-6-1998 and 25-6-1998 respectively. There-after, the petitioner submitted bill of entry for effecting release of two units Volvo Car from 1st consignment, all the two units Volvo Cars of 2nd consignment and two units Volvo Cars from 3rd consignments on 16-6-1998 when the rate of supplementary duty has been enhanced to @ 150% by the provision of Finance Act, 1998 and the same became leviable through the operation of Provisional Collection of Taxes Act from 1st June, 1998. Nothing appears from the Customs Nothi that any additional documents were asked from the petitioner or that the petitioner ever submitted any additional documents with his submission of bills of entry allegedly much earlier than 16-6-1998. Thereafter, we do not find any reason to treat these subsequent bills of entry as post-dated made by the respondents with an ulterior motive to collect duties at higher rates.

15. Secondly, from the Customs Nothi, we find that the Customs Authority on receiving the bills of entry on 16-6-1998 assessed the Customs Duty on 28-6-1998 and the petitioner obtained Rule Nisi on 25-8-1998 which was served upon the respondents on 7-9-1998. Thereafter, all the steps in the said Customs Nothi was stopped due to the pendency of the Rule. It further appears that petitioner after getting interim order in this Rule has taken release of only two units Volvo Cars as per the interim order of this Court and did not take release of remaining four units Volvo Cars in spite of the indulgence given by this Court to effect release of remaining six units Volvo Cars after furnishing appropriate Bank guarantee. The respondents although once took step to auction the said four units Volvo Cars under provision of section 82 of the Customs Act but considering the pendency of the instant Rule did not auction those cars which still remain with the Customs Custody.

16. Therefore, we do not find any substance in the contention of the petitioner that the Customs Authority having been empowered to take step under section 82 of the Customs Act, since failed to exercise such power, the same should not be treated in favour of the contention that the bills of entry were submitted by the petitioner much earlier than is showed by the Customs Authority as on 16-6-1998.

17. From section 82 of the Customs Act, 1969, we do not find that the same is non-relaxable provision so as to put the consignment on auction just after 45 days of its delivery in the Customs custody. Section 82 of the Customs Act runs as follows:

"82. Procedure in case of goods not cleared or warehoused or transhipped after unloading within a specified period—(1) If any goods are not entered and cleared for home consumption or warehoused or transhipped within forty-five days of the date of unloading thereof at a customs port or a land customs station, or within thirty days of the date of unloading thereof at a customs airport, or within such extended period as the appropriate officer may allow, such goods may, after due notice given to the owner, if his address could be ascertained or published in the newspaper, if his address could not be ascertained, be sold under the orders of the appropriate officer:

Provided that—

(a) animals and perishable and hazardous goods may, with the permission of the appropriate officer, be sold at any time;

(b) arms, ammunition or military stores may be sold or otherwise disposed of at such time and place and in such manner as the Board may, with the approval of the Government, direct."

Provided further that nothing in this section shall authorise removal for home consumption of any dutiable goods without payment of customs duties thereon.

(2) Where any goods are sold under sub-section (1) pending adjudication, appeal, revision or decision of a Court, the proceeds of such sale shall be deposited into the Government treasury and if, on such adjudication or in such appeal or revision, it is found or if the Court S finds that the goods so sold are not liable to confiscation the proceeds of the sale shall after necessary deduction of duties, taxes or dues as provided in section 201, be refunded to the owner.

<u>18. From bare reading of the section this Court has no hesitation to hold that the provision made therein regarding putting the imported consignment on auction due to failure of the importer to effect release of the goods within 45 days is relaxable provision as the time barrier may be extended by the appropriate officer of the Customs Authority. Therefore, we do not find any reason to rely on the analogy made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner to show that failure to put the consignment on auction by the Customs Authority just after 45 days, ipso facto, proves that the bills of entry was submitted much earlier than the date it shows on the body of bills of entry.</u>

<u>19. On the facts and circumstances of the case, we find that the petitioner submitted the bill of entry for effecting release of six units of Volvo Cars on 16-6-1998 and, therefore, liable to pay the duties and taxes prevailing on the said date and accordingly, the assessment made in the relevant Customs Nothi was made in accordance with law.</u>

20. Mr Morshed Ahmed Khan, in substantiating his contention that his vested right as to the rate of duty prevailing at the date when he opened the letter of credit cited the decision of the case of Cab Express (BD) Limited vs Commissioner of Customs and Nipun Cab Limited vs Commissioner of Customs reported in 9 BLC 398 in which one of us is the author Judge, we find that the facts of that case is quite distinguishable from the instant case and, as such, the principle enunciated in that case as to the vested right has no manner of application in this case.

21. On the discussion and reasoning as above, we find no merit in the instant Rule and, as such, it is liable to be discharged.

22. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The assessment made in the respective Customs Nothi regarding assessment of duties and taxes of six units of Volvo Cars covered by the bill of entry as aforesaid, is declared to be lawful.

However, there shall be no order as to cost.

End.
